p.src: Now Bajie and Sha Wujing fought the monster for some thirty rounds without either side gaining the upper hand. Why, you may ask, was there no victor? In sheer fighting skill, not merely these two monks but even twenty of them would have been no match for the fiend. But Tang Sanzang was not fated to die, and the guardian deities were secretly protecting him; and in the heavens the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Guardians of the Five Regions, the Duty Gods of the Four Watches, and the eighteen guardian arhats were lending aid to Bajie and Sha Wujing.

p.src: But let us leave the three of them fighting. The elder monk, meanwhile, was weeping sorrowfully inside the cave. Thinking of his disciples, he shed tears and said, “Wuneng, have you met some kindly friend in some village and lingered there over an offering of food? Wujing, where have you gone looking for him, and will you ever find him? How could you know that I have encountered a demon and am suffering here? When shall I see you again, escape this great calamity, and hasten on to Spirit Mountain?” As he grieved and fretted, a woman suddenly came out from within the cave. Supporting herself against the soul-fixing post, she called, “Elder, where have you come from? Why has he bound you here?” Hearing her, the elder peered through his tear-filled eyes and saw that she was about thirty years of age. He said, “Kind lady, there is no need to ask. I am doomed to die. Since I have walked into your home, eat me if you wish. Why ask any more?” The woman said, “I am not one who eats people. More than three hundred li west of here is my home, in a city called the Kingdom of Precious Image. I am that king’s third princess, and my childhood name is Baihuaxiu. Thirteen years ago, on the night of the fifteenth day of the eighth month, I was admiring the moon when this demon swept me away in a violent gust. I have lived here as his wife for thirteen years and borne his children, without any means of sending word back to the court. I long for my father and mother, but cannot see them. Where have you come from, and how did he capture you?” Tang Sanzang replied, “This poor monk was commissioned to journey to the Western Heaven for scriptures. While taking a short walk, I unexpectedly strayed here by mistake. Now he means to capture my two disciples as well and steam all three of us together for food.” The princess smiled courteously and said, “Set your mind at ease, Elder. Since you are a scripture pilgrim, I can save you. The Kingdom of Precious Image lies on the main road westward. Carry a letter there for me and present my respects to my parents, and I shall have him spare you.” Sanzang nodded. “Kind lady, if you can save this poor monk’s life, I shall gladly carry your letter and tidings.”

p.src: The princess hurried into the rear chamber, wrote a letter home, and sealed it securely. She returned to the post, released Tang Sanzang, and gave him the letter. Once freed, Tang Sanzang held the letter in both hands and said, “Kind lady, many thanks for saving my life. When I pass through your homeland, I shall certainly deliver it to the king. I fear only that after so many years your parents may refuse to acknowledge it. What then? You must not blame this poor monk for making an empty promise.” The princess said, “That will not matter. My royal father has no sons, only the three of us sisters. When he sees this letter, he will surely wish to receive you.” Sanzang tucked the family letter securely into his sleeve, thanked the princess, and started toward the front. The princess caught hold of him and said, “You cannot leave by the front gate. All the fiends, great and small, are outside waving banners and shouting, beating drums and clanging gongs as they cheer their king on in battle against your disciples. Go out by the rear gate. If the king catches you, he will at least question you first; but if one of the lesser fiends seizes you, I fear it will neither ask right from wrong nor show restraint, but kill you on the spot. Wait while I go and plead your case before him. If the king agrees to release you, I shall have your disciples informed so that they can find you and you may all leave together.” Hearing this, Sanzang bowed his head to the ground, obeyed her instructions, bade the princess farewell, and slipped out through the rear gate. Not daring to set off alone, he hid himself among the brambles.

p.src: The princess, having devised a clever plan, hurried to the front, went outside, and pushed her way through the assembled fiends, great and small. She heard only the ceaseless clang and clash of weapons. It was Bajie and Sha Wujing fighting the monster in midair. The princess cried out sharply, “Yellow-Robed One!” Hearing the princess call, the demon king immediately broke off his fight with Bajie and Sha Wujing and descended from the clouds. Lowering his steel saber, he supported the princess by the arm and asked, “Wife, what is it?” The princess said, “My husband, just now I was asleep behind the gauze curtains when suddenly, in a dream, I saw a divine being in golden armor.” The demon said, “What golden-armored god was that? What did he come to my gates for?” The princess replied, “When I was young and still living in the palace, I secretly made a vow before others: if I should win a worthy husband as prince consort, I would visit sacred mountains and immortal abodes, feed monks, and give alms. Since I became your wife, we have lived together happily, and to this day I have never mentioned it. The divine being in golden armor came to demand fulfillment of my vow and shouted me awake, whereupon I found it had all been a fleeting dream. So I hurriedly dressed and came to tell you, but then I happened to see a monk bound to that post. I earnestly beg you to show compassion and, for my humble sake, spare that monk. Let it count as my offering to a monk in fulfillment of the vow. Will you agree, my husband?” The monster replied, “Wife, you worry too much. It is hardly a matter of consequence. If I want human flesh, can I not catch a few people anywhere and eat them? What importance can this one monk have? Let him go.” The princess said, “My husband, let him leave by the rear gate.” The demon said, “What a nuisance! If he is to be freed, just let him go. Why bother about front gate or rear?” He raised his steel saber and shouted, “Zhu Bajie, come here! I am not refusing to fight because I fear you. For my wife’s sake, I shall spare your master. Go quickly to the rear gate, find him, and continue westward. If you ever trespass in my domain again, I shall show no mercy!”

He then reported, “This poor monk came first to have his documents endorsed and, second, because I carry a family letter for Your Majesty.” The king was delighted and asked, “What letter is that?” Tripitaka replied, “Your Majesty’s third daughter was abducted by the Yellow-Robed Demon of the Moon-Wave Cave on Bowl Mountain. This poor monk happened to meet her, and so she entrusted me with a letter.” At these words the king’s eyes brimmed with tears. “Since the princess disappeared thirteen years ago, I cannot tell how many civil and military officials have been demoted or dismissed, nor how many maids and eunuchs within and without the palace have been beaten to death. We thought only that she had left the palace, lost her way, and could nowhere be found. Countless households throughout the capital were questioned and searched, yet still no trace was discovered. p.src: After weeping for a long while, the king asked the assembled civil and military officials, “Who dares raise troops and lead our generals to capture the demon and rescue our Princess Hundred-Flowers?” He asked several times, but not one man dared answer. Truly, the generals might have been carved from wood and the civil officials molded from clay. The king was filled with distress, and his tears gushed like a spring. Then all the officials prostrated themselves together and reported, “Your Majesty, pray set aside your grief for the moment. The princess disappeared thirteen years ago and has not been heard from since. Now, by chance, she is said to have met this holy monk from Tang and sent a letter here, but we do not yet know whether the report is true. Moreover, we are all ordinary men mounted upon ordinary horses. We have studied military texts and strategy, but can only form battle lines, establish camps, and defend the realm from invasion. That fiend travels upon cloud and mist. If we cannot even come face-to-face with him, how could we march against him and effect a rescue? We understand that this pilgrim seeking scriptures from the Eastern Land is a holy monk of the superior realm. His Way is lofty enough to subdue dragons and tigers, and his virtue weighty enough to command the reverence of ghosts and gods; he must surely possess the art of conquering demons. As the old saying goes, ‘The man who brings word of trouble is himself involved in the trouble.’ We should therefore ask this elder to subdue the fiend and rescue the princess. That would surely be the safest plan.”

p.src: Hearing this, the king turned hastily to Tripitaka and implored him, “Elder, if you possess the skill, employ your magic powers to capture the demon and bring our child safely back to court. Then you need not journey west to worship the Buddha. Let your hair grow and leave the monkhood; we shall become sworn brothers, sit together upon the dragon throne, and share wealth and honor. What say you?” Tripitaka hurriedly replied, “This poor monk knows a little of reciting the Buddha’s name, but in truth I cannot subdue demons.” The king said, “If you cannot subdue demons, how do you dare journey to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha?” Unable to conceal the truth any longer, the elder told him about his two disciples. He reported, “Your Majesty, it would indeed have been difficult for this poor monk to come this far alone. This poor monk has two disciples who are skilled at opening roads through mountains and laying bridges wherever we meet water. They have protected me all the way here.” The king reproached him, “You monk are most unreasonable! Since you have disciples, why did you not bring them in with you to meet us? Though our court may have no reward entirely to their liking, we could at least provide a vegetarian meal befitting our means.” Tripitaka replied, “My disciples are ugly in appearance and dared not enter the court without leave, lest they frighten Your Majesty and harm your sacred person.” The king laughed. “Listen to how you speak, monk! Surely you do not think that we would be afraid of them?” Tripitaka said, “I scarcely dare describe them. My senior disciple’s surname is Zhu, and his names are Wuneng and Bajie. He has a long snout and tusks, stiff bristles and fanlike ears, a thick body and great belly, and he raises a wind as he walks. My second disciple’s surname is Sha, and his religious name is the monk Wujing. He stands twelve feet tall, with arms broad enough for three men; his face is as blue as indigo, his mouth like a basin of blood, his eyes flash with light, and his teeth are ranged like nails. Such are the appearances of them both, which is why I dared not bring them into court without permission.” The king said, “Now that you have described them so fully, why should we fear them? Summon them within.” A golden tally was immediately sent to the posthouse to invite them.

p.src: When the idiot heard that they had been invited, he said to Friar Sand, “Brother, you kept telling Master not to deliver the letter, but now you see the benefit of delivering it. I expect Master delivered the letter, and the king said that its bearer must not be neglected, so he is surely preparing a banquet for him. Master’s appetite is too feeble to manage it, and thinking kindly of you and me, he mentioned our names. That is why they have sent the golden tally to invite us. Let us all eat our fill, and tomorrow we can travel on.” Friar Sand said, “Brother, who knows what the true reason may be? Still, let us go and see.” They entrusted all the luggage and the horse to the posthouse keeper, each took his personal weapon, and followed the bearer of the golden tally into court. Soon they reached the white jade steps. Taking their places to left and right, they called out a greeting toward the throne and thereafter did not move. Every civil and military official was frightened by them. They all said, “It would be one thing if these two monks were merely ugly, but they are intolerably coarse! How can they appear before our king without kneeling, merely call out a greeting, then straighten up and stand there so brazenly? How extraordinary! How extraordinary!” Bajie overheard them and said, “Gentlemen, do not gossip about us. This is how we are: at first sight we admittedly look somewhat ugly, but after you have looked at us for a while, you will find us quite bearable.”

They all said, “It would be one thing if these two monks were merely ugly, but they are intolerably coarse! How can they appear before our king without kneeling, merely call out a greeting, then straighten up and stand there so brazenly?
How extraordinary! How extraordinary!”

Bajie overheard them and said, “Gentlemen, do not gossip about us. This is how we are: at first sight we admittedly look somewhat ugly, but after you have looked at us for a while, you will find us quite bearable.”

p.src: The king was already alarmed by his ugliness. When he heard the fool speak, he trembled all the more, lost his seat, and fell from the dragon throne. Fortunately, the attending officials caught and raised him. In his panic, the Tang monk knelt before the hall and repeatedly knocked his head upon the floor, saying, “Your Majesty, this poor monk deserves ten thousand deaths—ten thousand deaths! I told you my disciple was ugly and dared not bring him to court, lest the sight harm Your Majesty’s person; and indeed he has frightened you.” Still trembling, the king came forward and helped him up, saying, “Elder, it is fortunate that you warned me beforehand. Had you not done so, the sudden sight of him would surely have frightened me to death.” After taking a long while to compose himself, the king asked, “Elder Zhu and Elder Sha, which of you is skilled at subduing demons?” The fool, knowing no better, answered, “Old Zhu can subdue them.” The king asked, “How do you subdue them?” Bajie said, “I was once Marshal Tianpeng. Because I transgressed the laws of Heaven, I fell into the mortal world, but happily I have now returned to the true path and become a monk. Ever since we left the Eastern Land and came this far, I have been the foremost at subduing demons.” The king said, “Since you are a heavenly general descended to the mortal realm, you must surely be adept at transformations.” Bajie replied, “You flatter me. I do know a few transformations after a fashion.” The king said, “Show me one.” Bajie said, “Name what you want, so that I may transform myself accordingly.” The king said, “Then become something large.”

p.src: Bajie possessed thirty-six transformations. Showing off his powers before the steps, he formed a hand sign, recited a spell, and shouted, “Grow!” He bent his back and grew to a height of eighty or ninety feet, like a gigantic road-clearing deity. The civil and military officials in both ranks trembled with fear, and the sovereign and all his ministers stared in stupefaction. Then a general guarding the hall asked, “Elder, when you make yourself so tall, how far must you grow before reaching your limit?” The fool gave another foolish answer: “That depends on the wind. An east wind is tolerable, and I can manage with a west wind too; but if a south wind rises, I shall thrust a great hole right through the blue heavens.” Greatly alarmed, the king said, “Put away your magic. I understand now what sort of transformations you can perform.” Bajie shrank his body, resumed his original form, and stood in attendance before the steps.

p.src: The king asked again, “Elder, what weapon will you take to fight him?” Bajie pulled the rake from his belt and said, “Old Zhu uses this rake.” The king laughed. “That will make a sorry display. I have whips, iron rods, maces and hammers, sabers, spears, battle-axes and axes, swords, halberds, lances and sickles. Choose whichever suits your hand and take it. What sort of weapon is a rake?” Bajie said, “Your Majesty does not know. Though this rake looks crude and clumsy, it has been my personal weapon since my youth. When I commanded the River of Heaven’s watery domain and governed eighty thousand marines, I relied wholly upon the might of this rake. Now that I have descended to the mortal world to protect my master, I use this rake to smash the lairs of tigers and wolves whenever we meet mountains, and overturn the dens of dragons and sea monsters whenever we meet water.”

p.src: Hearing this, the king was delighted and believed him completely. He at once commanded his imperial consorts, “Bring a whole bottle of the wine reserved for my own use, as a parting gift for the elder.” He filled a goblet to the brim and presented it to Bajie, saying, “Elder, let this cup convey a small token of my gratitude for your trouble. When you have captured the demon and rescued my daughter, I shall reward you with a great banquet and a thousand pieces of gold.” The fool took the cup. Though rough in appearance, he could be courteous in his conduct. Making a deep bow to Tripitaka, he said, “Master, by rights you should drink first; but as the sovereign bestowed it upon me, I dare not refuse. Let Old Zhu drink first to raise his spirits for catching the demon.” The fool drained it in one swallow, then poured another cup and handed it to his master. Tripitaka said, “I do not drink wine. You brothers may have it.” Sha Monk stepped forward and took it. Bajie summoned a cloud beneath his feet and rose straight into the sky. Seeing this, the king said, “Elder Zhu can ride the clouds as well?”

p.src: After the fool had departed, Sha Monk also drained the wine in one swallow and said, “Master, when the Yellow-Robed Monster captured you, the two of us fought him and could only manage a draw. Now that Second Brother has gone alone, I fear he will be unable to defeat him.” Tripitaka said, “Quite so. Disciple, go and lend him your aid.” On hearing this, Sha Monk too leapt onto a cloud and soared away. The king panicked, seized the Tang monk, and said, “Elder, stay and sit with me awhile. You must not ride away on a cloud too.” The Tang monk said, “Alas, alas! I cannot travel even half a step that way.” For the moment, we leave the two conversing in the hall.

p.src: Now Sha Monk caught up with Bajie and called, “Brother, I have come!” Bajie asked, “Brother, what have you come for?” Sha Monk replied, “Master told me to come and help you.” Bajie was delighted. “He was right, and you are most welcome. If the two of us strive together with one heart to capture that monster, even if we accomplish nothing remarkable, we shall at least make our names known throughout this kingdom.” Just look at them:

p.src: Before long, the two reached the cave entrance and brought their clouds down. Bajie drew his rake and struck the gate of the Moon-Wave Cave with all his might, smashing a hole in the stone door as large as a bushel measure. The gatekeeping imp was so frightened that he opened the door; seeing the two of them, he rushed inside and reported, “Disaster, Great King! The monk with the long snout and big ears and the monk with the dark, ill-favored face have returned and smashed our gate!” The monster said in surprise, “Those must be Zhu Bajie and Sha Monk. I spared their master, so how dare they return and attack my gate?” The imp said, “Perhaps they forgot something and have come back to fetch it.” The old monster barked, “Nonsense! Would they storm my gate merely because they forgot something? There must be some reason.” He hastily put his armor in order, snatched up his steel saber, and strode out to ask, “You monks! Since I spared your master, how dare you return and attack my gate?” Bajie said, “You wretched monster, what a fine deed you have done!” The old demon asked, “What deed?” Bajie said, “You tricked the third princess of the Kingdom of Precious Image into your cave and, relying on brute force, took her as your wife. You have kept her for thirteen years, and it is time to return her. By the king’s command, I have come expressly to capture you. Hurry inside, bind yourself with rope, and come out; then Old Zhu will not have to lay hands on you.” Hearing this, the old monster flew into a terrible rage. See how fiercely he bristled and ground his steel-hard teeth; how wildly his round, ringed eyes glared; how boldly he raised his saber; and how savagely he brought it straight down upon Bajie’s head. Bajie twisted aside to evade the blow and met him face-on with his rake; behind him, Sha Monk rushed forward and joined the attack with his precious staff raised. This contest upon the mountaintop was quite unlike their previous battle. Truly it was a sight to behold:

p.src: They fought for eight or nine rounds before the mountainside. Bajie gradually began to fail; he could scarcely raise his rake, and his strength was ebbing. Why, you may ask, were they now unable to overcome him? When they fought him the first time, the guardian deities had secretly aided Bajie and Sha Monk because the Tang monk was inside the cave, and thus they had just managed a draw; but now all the deities were in the Kingdom of Precious Image guarding the Tang monk, so the two disciples found the monster hard to withstand.

p.src: The fool said, “Sha Monk, go forward and keep him fighting while old Pig goes to relieve himself.” Without another thought for Sha Monk, he darted into the mugwort, vines, thornbushes, and tangled creepers, plunging headlong through them without caring where he went. He cared nothing if his scalp was torn or his face and mouth were pierced; he rolled down and lay there, not daring to come out again. He merely left half an ear uncovered to listen for the sound of the clapper.
